newsitem.title: UK: Peru siege may spark market sell-off, investors say.
newsitem.headline: Peru siege may spark market sell-off, investors say.

text.p: The guerrilla seige of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima will damage investor perceptions of Peru, fund managers said on Wednesday, and they predicted a knee-jerk stock market reaction on Wall Street.

"There was a feeling that (President Alberto) Fujimori was on top of the guerrilla problem -- clearly this is going to do a lot of damage to that perception," said Neil Dougall, Latin America economist at Kleinwort Benson Securities in London.
"The break-through on terrorism was supposed to be his big plus point -- this is bad news from that point of view."
A band of about 20 heavily armed guerrillas staged a spectacular attack on a reception hosted by the Japanese ambassador at his Lima residence late on Tuesday.
They took some 200 high-ranking foreign diplomats, business officials and journalists hostage, threatening to kill them unless the government releases jailed comrades.

Philip Ehrmann, head of global emerging markets at Gartmore Investment Management in London, said there would be an initial emotional reaction among foreign investors in response to television pictures of the seige, though he doubted there would be a long term impact.
"This is just a psychological body blow -- there will be an emotional reaction and a sell-off in response to the CNN pictures in New York," he said.
But he added that longer term it would not make people invest there any less.
Recently privatised Telefonica del Peru looked likely to feel the brunt of investor reaction especially when the big U.S. players weigh in.
"The stock is large, liquid and very visible -- any reaction in the market will be more than reflected in the stock," Ehrmann said.
"It is reasonably attractive at current levels and if it sells off very sharply then it will be even more attractive, provided you're prepared to take a medium-term view," he added.
Telefonica del Peru shares closed up one eighth at 19-1/4 on Tuesday, after reaching a high this year of 24-2/8.
"I wouldn't be surprised if it goes lower," said one fund manager at a rival firm. "If it goes say to 17 then I'm a buyer."
Brady debt market investors in London were sanguine, saying they were aware of on-going rebel problems in Peru and did not expect the guerrilla stand-off to affect prices.

Most were more interested in news late on Tuesday that the World Bank is set to approve a $283 million loan, the bulk of which will go towards start-up costs for a plan to restructure its foreign commercial debt.

Many investors had believed Mexico and Colombia were more at risk from a resurgence in guerrilla violence than Peru, which was seen to have largely eradicated the threat of its Shining Path rebels after arresting their leader Abimael Guzman in 1992.

Once Latin America's strongest growing economy, clocking up nearly 13 percent in 1994, investors are expecting a growth slowdown to this year to around 2.0 percent before a pick-up in 1997. Forecasts for next year range from 4.6 to 5.0 percent.

They maintain their watch on its inflation rate, with the central bank aiming for 11.2 percent in 1996, and its current account and trade deficits. "A growth slow-down is necessary to keep the trade deficit under control," Dougall said.
